statement: As described in an American Heart Association scientific statement and in narrative reviews (all figures second-hand; no primary study was read here, and the statement gives no search or appraisal method), studies of adults who use cannabis point in different directions on heart attack, stroke and other heart and blood-vessel disease, and the AHA writing group judged the evidence still inconclusive (Page et al., 2020). In the hour after use, the risk of a heart attack starting was 4.8 times that at other times in a case-crossover study of 3,882 people with a heart attack, an estimate printed without an interval that rests on the 9 people who had used cannabis in that hour (Mittleman et al., 2001, as relayed by Page et al., 2020, and Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015, calls it a quadrupling). Two surveys found more stroke: past-year use went with 3.3 times the rate of stroke or transient ischaemic attack, 2.3 (95% CI 1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related factors including tobacco smoking, with the excess confined to weekly or more frequent use (4.7, 2.1 to 10.7; adjustment not stated) (Hemachandra et al., 2016); and among adults aged 18 to 44, use went with an adjusted OR for stroke of 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10), and 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) with use on more than 10 days a month (Parekh et al.; adjustment set not stated). Health-record and hospital databases report more heart attacks where cannabis use is recorded, for example 1.37% against 0.54% over 3 years (about 14 against 5 in 1,000, editors' conversion; RR 2.53, adjustment not stated; Chami & Kim, 2019), but the statement warns that samples of hospitalised patients carry a high probability of selection bias. Against these, in the CARDIA cohort (5,113 adults aged 18 to 30 at the start, followed for more than 25 years) cumulative lifetime and recent use were not associated with new cardiovascular disease, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, coronary heart disease or cardiac death (Reis et al., 2017; no estimates printed), and after a heart attack long-term mortality was 29% higher in people who used cannabis but not significantly (95% CI 0.81 to 2.05; adjustment not stated; Frost et al., 2013). Laboratory studies show dose-related rises in heart rate, to which healthy young adults quickly become tolerant, and angina brought on by smoking cannabis in people with heart disease (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Page et al., 2020). The statement names short-term, observational and retrospective designs, poorly measured exposure, recall bias, low-risk cohorts and confounding by tobacco as the main weaknesses, and judges the evidence for people with cardiac risk factors insufficient; Hall (2015) concludes that cannabis smoking by middle-aged adults probably increases the risk of heart attack. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does cannabis cause heart attacks or strokes? This has not been shown. In one study, a heart attack was more likely to start in the hour after using cannabis, and two surveys found more strokes, mostly in people who used cannabis every week or more. Hospital records also show more heart attacks in people who use cannabis, but these records are hard to interpret. A study that followed young adults for over 25 years found no link with heart disease or stroke. In lab studies, cannabis raised heart rate and brought on chest pain (angina) in people with heart disease. The American Heart Association called the evidence inconclusive. These figures come from reviews, not from the studies themselves, and the studies could not fully separate cannabis from tobacco. See the contested question.
population: Adults in studies relayed by an American Heart Association statement and narrative reviews: people with a heart attack (a US case-crossover study and its follow-up), population survey samples, US hospital and health-record databases, and young US adults in the CARDIA cohort
exposure: Cannabis use as each relayed study recorded it: use in the hour before a heart attack (case-crossover); past-year use, weekly or more, or more than 10 days a month (stroke surveys); recorded use or diagnosis codes (hospital databases); cumulative lifetime and recent use (CARDIA)
comparator: The same people at other times (case-crossover); people without reported or recorded use in the same survey, cohort or database; placebo in laboratory studies
outcome: Onset of heart attack; stroke or transient ischaemic attack; heart attacks in hospital records; new cardiovascular disease, coronary heart disease and cardiac death; death after a heart attack; heart rate and angina
magnitude: All second-hand. Case-crossover (Mittleman et al. 2001, 3,882 people with a heart attack): onset 4.8 times baseline in the 60 minutes after use (no interval; 9 people had used cannabis in that hour); follow-up of 1,913: mortality over 3.8 years 2.5 times with use less than weekly and 4.2 times with use more than weekly (as relayed by Hall & Degenhardt 2009). Stroke: Hemachandra et al. 2016, past-year use, rate ratio 3.3 (1.8 to 6.3) unadjusted and 2.3 (1.1 to 4.5) adjusted including tobacco, 4.7 (2.1 to 10.7) for weekly or more frequent use; Parekh et al., adults aged 18 to 44, adjusted OR 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10), 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) for use on more than 10 days a month, 3.12 (1.40 to 6.97) with combustible cigarettes and 2.63 (1.07 to 6.46) with e-cigarettes. Databases: Chami & Kim 2019, 3-year heart-attack incidence 1.37% vs 0.54% (about 14 vs 5 in 1,000, editors' conversion), RR 2.53 (2.45 to 2.61); Desai et al. 2019, heart-attack admissions of young adults 0.23% vs 0.14%. CARDIA (Reis et al. 2017, 5,113 adults, over 25 years): no association, no estimates printed. After a heart attack: Frost et al. 2013, mortality 29% higher, 95% CI 0.81 to 2.05, P = 0.28; Johnson-Sasso et al. 2018, in-hospital mortality OR 0.79. Laboratory: exercise time to angina 48% shorter after one cannabis cigarette than after placebo.

evidence.extracted: Method as stated: the writing group describes the statement as a critical review of medicinal and recreational cannabis from clinical, policy and public-health perspectives, focused on cardiovascular health; no search strategy, databases, dates, inclusion criteria, appraisal method or grading system is described; it was approved by two AHA committees and peer-reviewed through the AHA by four named reviewers.

evidence.page: pp. e9–e10 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 2nd paragraph (p. e9), 3rd paragraph (starts p. e9) and 4th paragraph (p. e10)
evidence.extracted: Weaknesses the statement names: most data are short-term, observational and retrospective, with poorly determined exposure, recall bias, minimal exposure without dose or product standardisation and typically low-risk cohorts; epidemiological studies may be confounded by access to health care and other behaviours such as tobacco use; rising THC content may make earlier studies less relevant; few data come from rigorous prospective cohorts; signals for adverse cardiac outcomes come mostly from hospitalised patients, where a high probability of selection bias makes cannabis as a cause of hospitalisation uncertain; and concomitant tobacco and other drug use is inadequately handled in data collection and statistical adjustment.

evidence.page: pp. e12, e17 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Table 3, row Mittleman et al (p. e12); Considerations in Special Populations › Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease, paragraph (p. e17)
evidence.extracted: As relayed (Mittleman et al., case-crossover design, 3882 patients with acute myocardial infarction): risk of infarction onset 4.8 times baseline in the 60 minutes after cannabis use (no interval printed); 3% of the patients had smoked cannabis in the prior year, 37 within 24 hours and 9 within 1 hour of presentation; people who used cannabis were more likely to be men, cigarette smokers and obese.

evidence.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 7th paragraph (left column)
evidence.extracted: As summarized: evidence exists to support adverse cardiovascular effects; cannabis and THC raise heart rate in a dose-dependent way, marginally affecting healthy young adults, who quickly develop tolerance, with concern for adults with cardiovascular disease. In a case-crossover study of 3882 people who had had a myocardial infarction, cannabis use increased the risk of infarction 4.8 times in the hour after use; a prospective study of 1913 of them found a dose–response relation with mortality over 3.8 years, risk 2.5 times with use less than once a week and 4.2 times with use more than once a week; laboratory studies show that smoking cannabis provokes angina in people with heart disease.

evidence.locator: Cardiovascular effects, 1st paragraph (begins p. 9, continues p. 10) and 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 10); Table 1 and WHAT HAVE WE LEARNED IN 20 YEARS? › Physical health outcomes (p. 12)
evidence.extracted: As summarized: in 1993 laboratory studies showed dose-related rises in heart rate with rapid tolerance in healthy young adults, and angina in older adults with cardiovascular disease; the evidence has not increased a great deal since, but is called consistent with adverse cardiovascular effects in middle-aged and older adults. The same case-crossover study of 3882 people is said to show the risk of infarction quadrupled in the hour after smoking, and its follow-up of 1913 a dose–response with mortality over 3.8 years; a French series of 200 cannabis-related hospitalisations (Toulouse area, January 2004 to December 2007) included several infarctions and a fatal stroke in young adults with recent use and no other known risk factors. Table 1 gives the strength of effect for cardiovascular disease as 3–4-fold for myocardial infarction (its symbols are undefined), and the conclusions say cannabis smoking by middle-aged adults probably increases the risk of myocardial infarction.

evidence.page: pp. e10, e12, e14, e17 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 5th paragraph (p. e10); Table 3, row Hemachandra et al (p. e12); Considerations in Special Populations › Young Adults, paragraph (p. e14); Patients With Cardiac Risk Factors, paragraph (p. e17)
evidence.extracted: As relayed: in a population survey (PATH Through Life, age cohorts 20–24, 40–44 and 60–64, surveyed 1999–2002; Hemachandra et al.), people with past-year cannabis use (n = 1043) had 3.3 times the rate of stroke or transient ischaemic attack (95% CI 1.8 to 6.3), a rate ratio of 2.3 (1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related covariates including tobacco smoking, with stroke or TIA in people using weekly or more often (4.7, 2.1 to 10.7) and no elevation at lower frequency. In the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, among adults aged 18 to 44 (Parekh et al.), the adjusted OR for stroke was 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10) for people who used marijuana against those who did not, 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) for use on more than 10 days a month, 3.12 (1.40 to 6.97) for frequent use with combustible cigarettes and 2.63 (1.07 to 6.46) with e-cigarettes; adjustment sets not stated. The text and Table 3 give different cohort sizes (study card reporting issue).

evidence.page: p. e11 of the online-first PDF
evidence.locator: Table 3, rows Chami and Kim and Desai et al (ref 33)
evidence.extracted: As relayed: in an aggregate multi-institutional health-record database (Explorys, 2011–2016), people with a history of cannabis use (labelled the cannabis abuse group) had, against more than 10 million controls, a 3-year cumulative incidence of acute myocardial infarction of 1.37% against 0.54% (RR 2.53, 95% CI 2.45 to 2.61; adjustment not stated). In the National Inpatient Sample 2007–2014 (more than 52 million hospitalisations; cannabis use without other substance use), admissions for myocardial infarction in young adults were 0.23% against 0.14%, arrhythmia and stroke were more frequent and venous thromboembolism less frequent in people who used cannabis (editors' conversion of the first pair: about 14 and 5 in 1,000).

evidence.extracted: As relayed: a systematic review of 85 studies, case reports and case series (Richards et al.) found that 28 of 33 studies evaluated suggested an increased risk of both acute coronary syndrome and chronic cardiovascular disease from cannabis use; of 51 case reports or series with 62 people, 21 (34%) had cardiomyopathy and 14 deaths (23%) were attributed to acute coronary syndrome.

evidence.extracted: As relayed: among 3886 people who had had a myocardial infarction (Frost et al., Determinants of MI Onset Study, National Death Index), mortality was 29% higher in people who used cannabis than in those who did not, not statistically significant (95% CI 0.81 to 2.05; P = 0.28). In hospital records from 8 states, 1994–2013, of more than 1.2 million patients with myocardial infarction, 3854 (about 0.3%) reported cannabis use; the composite primary outcome (death, intra-aortic balloon pump, mechanical ventilation, cardiac arrest, shock) was not associated with cannabis use and mortality was lower (OR 0.79, no interval).

risk_of_bias.note: Not appraisable at the level of the primary studies: the AHA statement gives no search, selection rule or appraisal (card sc_page_2020: overall high) and the narrative reviews are unsystematic (cards sc_hall_2009, sc_hall_2015, sc_volkow_2014). The relayed studies are mostly hospital databases with selection bias, surveys with self-reported use and case reports, with adjustment unstated in most and tobacco use inadequately handled, as the statement itself says.

inconsistency.note: The long prospective cohort found no association while the case-crossover, survey and database studies did; outcomes after a heart attack run both ways (non-significantly higher long-term mortality, lower in-hospital mortality); one case-crossover estimate is given as 4.8 times, a quadrupling and 3–4-fold by the reviews.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: every figure is a review's account of studies not read here (METHODS §6.3), and several rows of the statement's table cannot be right as printed (card sc_page_2020, reporting issues).

imprecision.note: The trigger estimate rests on 9 exposed people and has no interval; stroke intervals are wide (2.1 to 10.7; 1.08 to 3.10); the CARDIA null is printed without estimates, so its precision is unknown.

large_effect.note: The 4.8-fold trigger estimate rests on 9 exposed people, without an interval or adjustment; no upgrade.

dose_response.note: Gradients by frequency (mortality after a heart attack; stroke with weekly or more frequent use) come second-hand from single studies without stated adjustment; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence seen only through reviews starts low and is downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision: very low, the floor. Overlapping sources are counted once: Hall & Degenhardt (2009), Hall (2015) and the AHA statement relay the same case-crossover study and its mortality follow-up, and the statement's inpatient analyses largely share one database. Contested because credible designs disagree (the long cohort against the trigger, survey and database studies) and the reviews read the same evidence differently (still inconclusive for the AHA; probable for middle-aged adults in Hall, 2015). The claim rests only on second-hand sources (a professional statement without a stated search, and narrative reviews), so it stays at draft and says so (METHODS §6.3).

debate.question: Does using cannabis raise the risk of heart attack, stroke or other heart and blood-vessel disease?
debate.evidence_yes: In a case-crossover study of 3,882 people with a heart attack, the risk of onset in the 60 minutes after cannabis use was 4.8 times baseline; 37 had used cannabis within 24 hours and 9 within 1 hour of presentation (Mittleman et al., as relayed by Page et al., 2020, and Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), and in a follow-up of 1,913 of them mortality over 3.8 years rose with frequency of use, 2.5 times with use less than weekly and 4.2 times with use more than weekly (as relayed by Hall & Degenhardt, 2009). In a population survey, past-year use went with 3.3 times the rate of stroke or transient ischaemic attack and a rate ratio of 2.3 (1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment that included tobacco, the excess lying in weekly or more frequent use (4.7, 2.1 to 10.7); in a US survey of adults aged 18 to 44 the adjusted OR for stroke was 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10), and 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) with use on more than 10 days a month (both as relayed by Page et al., 2020). A health-record database found a 3-year incidence of heart attack of 1.37% against 0.54% (RR 2.53, 2.45 to 2.61), an inpatient database found heart-attack admissions of young adults of 0.23% against 0.14% among people using cannabis without other substances, and a systematic review of studies and case reports found that 28 of 33 studies suggested a higher risk of both acute coronary syndrome and chronic cardiovascular disease (all as relayed by Page et al., 2020). Laboratory studies show dose-related rises in heart rate and angina brought on by smoking cannabis in people with heart disease, exercise time to angina falling by 48% against placebo in one. Hall (2015) reads the evidence as consistent with adverse cardiovascular effects in middle-aged and older adults, adds a French series of cannabis-related hospitalisations that included heart attacks and a fatal stroke in young adults with no other known risk factors, and concludes that cannabis smoking by middle-aged adults probably increases the risk of heart attack; Volkow et al. (2014) describe use as associated with vascular conditions that raise the risk of heart attack, stroke and transient ischaemic attack during intoxication.
debate.evidence_no: In the CARDIA cohort, 5,113 adults aged 18 to 30 at the 1985–1986 baseline and followed for more than 25 years, cumulative lifetime and recent use were not associated with new cardiovascular disease, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, coronary heart disease or cardiac death (Reis et al., as relayed by Page et al., 2020), and in the same cohort higher aortic and coronary calcium went with cannabis only in people who had ever smoked tobacco (Auer et al., 3,498 participants). After a heart attack, long-term mortality was 29% higher in people who used cannabis but not significantly (95% CI 0.81 to 2.05; 3,886 patients; Frost et al.), and in hospital records of more than 1.2 million heart-attack patients the composite in-hospital outcome was not associated with cannabis use and in-hospital mortality was lower (OR 0.79; Johnson-Sasso et al.). The AHA statement warns that studies restricted to hospitalised patients carry a high probability of selection bias, so cannabis as a cause of hospitalisation is uncertain; that most data are short-term, observational and retrospective, with poorly determined exposure, recall bias and low-risk cohorts; and that tobacco and other drug use are inadequately handled in data collection and adjustment, 97% of people who smoke cannabis also smoking tobacco in the literature on cannabis arteritis. The 4.8-fold trigger estimate has no printed interval and rests on 9 exposed people, the 4.7 estimate for weekly use has no stated adjustment, and the database estimates are crude or silent on adjustment (Page et al., 2020). The AHA writing group judges the evidence still inconclusive overall and insufficient for people with cardiac risk factors.
debate.neither_can_show: Whether cannabis itself causes any of these events: none of the relayed studies convincingly separates cannabis from tobacco, which most people who smoke cannabis also use, or from other drugs, and none is a sibling comparison or a genetically informed design. The case-crossover design removes stable differences between people, but it concerns the minutes to hours after use and rests on 9 exposed people and on their recall of timing, while CARDIA concerns decades of use in young adults with few events, so the two results need not conflict. Whether results from smoked cannabis apply to eating or vaping it, and whether older studies apply to today's stronger products, which the statement itself questions. How large any risk is for a given person: no source gives absolute rates by age and baseline risk. All figures here are second-hand, and several rows of the statement's own table cannot be right as printed (card sc_page_2020).
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). From second-hand sources only: the clearest signal is short-lived, a higher chance of a heart attack starting in the hour after use, from one case-crossover study with few exposed people, together with laboratory evidence that cannabis raises heart rate and can bring on angina in people with heart disease. Signals for stroke come from two surveys and lie mainly in frequent use; the hospital-database associations are hard to read because of selection bias, unstated adjustment and tobacco. The one long cohort of young adults found no association with new heart disease or stroke over 25 years, which fits a short-lived trigger as well as no effect, because such a cohort has few events. The AHA judges the evidence inconclusive and, for people with cardiac risk factors, insufficient, and the editors agree that no long-term risk figure can be given from these sources. The primary studies themselves have not been read for this page.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Large prospective cohorts, or a pooled analysis of existing ones, with repeated measures of how often, by which route and how strong the cannabis used is, and of tobacco, analysed separately in people who have never smoked tobacco, with confirmed heart attacks, strokes, rhythm problems and cardiac deaths and absolute risks by age and baseline risk; case-crossover studies with objectively timed use; sibling or genetically informed designs; and a systematic review with a stated search and risk-of-bias appraisal to bring them together (the AHA statement calls for carefully designed prospective short- and long-term studies).

statement: In observational samples of people who used cannabis regularly or had a cannabis use disorder, the share with cannabis withdrawal, as each study defined it, depended strongly on where the sample came from, in a 2020 meta-analysis of 50 cohorts with 23,518 participants (searched to June 2019; Bahji et al., 2020; AMSTAR 2 critically low; English only; no group of people who did not cut down for comparison): 17 in 100 (95% CI 13 to 22) in 15 general-population samples holding 17,475 people, 54 in 100 (48 to 59) in 28 outpatient samples (5,684 people) and 87 in 100 (79 to 94) in 7 inpatient or residential samples (357 people). Withdrawal at any time in life was reported far more often than withdrawal in the past year (76 in 100, 70 to 82, in 18 cohorts, against 31 in 100, 27 to 36, in 32), and the one general-population sample assessed with DSM-5 criteria found it in 12.1% of 1,527 people. The review's headline figure, 47 in 100 (41 to 52; I2 99.2%; cohorts from 8% to 100%), is close to the plain average of the cohort estimates and is driven by small clinical samples; the review's own count, 6,469 of 23,518 participants, is about 27.5 in 100 (editors' calculation on the study card). Men and women did not differ (27 and 26 in 100, 15 studies), although the review's conclusions say withdrawal was more common in men. In DSM-5, cannabis withdrawal means at least three of seven symptoms within about a week of stopping or cutting down: irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep difficulty; less appetite or weight loss; restlessness; low mood; and physical symptoms such as headache, sweating or stomach pain (as summarised by Bahji et al., 2020, and Connor et al., 2021). As described in narrative reviews, whose figures are second-hand, symptoms typically begin 1 to 2 days after stopping, peak within the first week (at 2 to 6 days in one account) and fade within 1 to 2 weeks (Curran et al., 2016; Connor et al., 2021); craving, nightmares and nausea are also prominent, and THC relieves the symptoms in a dose-dependent way (Curran et al., 2016); people seeking help to stop most often report anxiety, sleep problems, appetite disturbance and low mood (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), often severe enough to impair everyday life (Hall, 2015); one review gives around half of people who use daily as having withdrawal when they stop, citing an earlier review (Curran et al., 2016); and in people without other medical or psychiatric illness withdrawal is described as carrying no serious risk and usually needing only supportive care (Connor et al., 2021). Sleep after stopping is covered in more detail in the claims on sleep. The cohorts defined regular use differently, most predate DSM-5, the review took the lowest threshold where studies offered several, cohorts with more tobacco use reported more withdrawal (a comparison between studies), and in people who use both daily, stopping both gives stronger symptoms than stopping either alone (Curran et al., 2016). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: When people who use cannabis regularly stop or cut down, some get withdrawal: irritability or anger, nervousness, poor sleep, less appetite, restlessness, low mood, or physical symptoms such as headaches. A 2020 review found it in about 17 in 100 people with regular use in general-population surveys, 54 in 100 in outpatient groups and 87 in 100 in inpatient groups; withdrawal at any time in life was reported much more often than in the past year. Reviews say it usually starts 1 to 2 days after stopping, is worst in the first week and fades within 1 to 2 weeks, and that it carries no serious medical risk for people without other illnesses. The studies defined regular use and withdrawal in different ways, and none checked how often the same feelings occur in people who do not cut down.
population: People with regular cannabis use or a cannabis use disorder in 50 observational cohorts (15 general-population, 28 outpatient, 7 inpatient or residential; 38 from North America), and people seeking help to stop, as described in narrative reviews
exposure: Stopping or cutting down after regular use (regular use as each cohort defined it; the review gives no common definition)
comparator: None (prevalence without a comparison group); settings and timeframes compared with each other
outcome: Cannabis withdrawal syndrome as each study defined it (DSM-5 in 5 cohorts, mostly earlier research definitions), at any time in life or in the past year; symptoms and time course as described in reviews
magnitude: Bahji 2020, random-effects pooled prevalence: general population 17% (95% CI 13 to 22; 15 cohorts; 17,475 people; I2 98%); outpatient 54% (48 to 59; 28; 5,684); inpatient 87% (79 to 94; 7; 357); past year 31% (27 to 36; 32 cohorts); lifetime 76% (70 to 82; 18); overall 47% (41 to 52; 50 cohorts; I2 99.2%; range 8% to 100%); men 27% (21 to 34), women 26% (19 to 33), P = .99; one DSM-5 population cohort 12.1% of 1,527. Editors' calculation on the card: 6,470 of 23,518 participants (27.5%). Time course as described in reviews: onset 1-2 days (24-48 hours), peak within the first week (2-6 days), resolution within 1-2 weeks.

evidence.locator: Diagnosis, screening and prevention › Diagnostic systems, 3rd paragraph; Management › Cannabis withdrawal, 1st-2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: DSM-5 withdrawal: within a week of stopping, three or more of irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep problems; reduced appetite or weight loss; restlessness; low mood; and a physical symptom, with clinically significant distress or impairment. Second-hand: symptoms typically begin 24-48 hours after stopping, peak within the first week and last 1-2 weeks; 12% of people who use frequently had DSM-5 withdrawal in the past 12 months in a US national sample; 54% of outpatients and 87% of inpatients (from Bahji et al.); without medical or psychiatric comorbidity withdrawal poses no serious risk and most people need only supportive care.

evidence.locator: Cannabis addiction and withdrawal, 2nd paragraph (p. 299); References 71 to 73 and 77 (p. 304)
evidence.extracted: Second-hand: a withdrawal syndrome said to affect around 50% of people who use daily when they stop, typically beginning 1-2 days after stopping, peaking at 2-6 days and fading by 1-2 weeks (ref 71, a 2004 review by Budney and colleagues); prominent symptoms craving, sleep problems, nightmares, anger, irritability, dysphoria and nausea (ref 72, Allsop and colleagues, 2011); symptoms can be relieved by THC in a dose-dependent way (ref 73); in people who use cannabis and tobacco daily, combined withdrawal is stronger than withdrawal from either alone (ref 77).

evidence.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 3rd paragraph (p. 1386); Reference 40 (p. 1390)
evidence.extracted: Second-hand: people seeking help to stop report withdrawal symptoms including anxiety, insomnia, appetite disturbance and depression (ref 40, Budney & Hughes, 2006); tolerance to many effects of THC develops in animals and humans, and a cannabinoid-receptor blocker brings on a withdrawal syndrome in rats, mice and dogs that THC reverses.

evidence.locator: Cannabis dependence, 3rd paragraph (p. 5); References 44 to 46 (p. 14)
evidence.extracted: Second-hand: the evidence for a withdrawal syndrome is said to have strengthened since 1993; people who seek help often report symptoms that make abstinence harder, most commonly anxiety, insomnia, appetite disturbance and depression (ref 44, Budney & Hughes, 2006), often severe enough to impair everyday functioning (ref 45, Allsop and colleagues, 2012); a double-blind trial found the symptoms markedly reduced by a cannabis extract (ref 46, nabiximols, 2014).

evidence.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF ADDICTION, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Second-hand: a withdrawal syndrome (irritability, sleep difficulties, dysphoria, craving, anxiety) is described as recognised, as making cessation difficult and as contributing to relapse.

risk_of_bias.note: Cohorts mostly rated fair (36 of 50) or poor (12) on the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale; clinical and residential samples selected for heavy use; lifetime withdrawal recalled in surveys; the lowest available threshold used; no comparison group to subtract background symptoms; the review is AMSTAR 2 critically low (card sc_bahji_2020).

inconsistency.note: I2 99.2% overall and 98% within general-population samples, whose estimates run from 7.6% to 34.4%; two analyses of one national survey gave 8.0% and 34.4%. Setting and timeframe explain part of the spread, not all.

indirectness.note: Regular use undefined; most definitions predate DSM-5; the pools include a prison survey and a synthetic-cannabinoid detoxification sample; the symptom description and time course are second-hand (narrative reviews).

imprecision.note: The setting estimates have intervals a few points wide.

publication_bias.note: Tests reported as negative (supplement not read); of little meaning for prevalence estimates.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (prevalence in the populations sampled): starts low; down one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low. The headline 47% is not used as the answer, because it averages cohorts of very different kinds and tracks the average cohort rather than the average participant (card sc_bahji_2020); the setting-specific figures are. The narrative reviews describe symptoms and time course second-hand and overlap with the meta-analysis (Connor et al., 2021, take their 54% and 87% from it), so they are not counted as further studies. Status replicated: in 50 cohorts from many teams withdrawal was found in some people who used regularly, consistently more often in clinical samples; how often varies widely, which the inconsistency rating carries.

verification.flag_note: Draft. Prevalence rests on one meta-analysis (card sc_bahji_2020, PMC, first-pass); symptoms and time course are second-hand from narrative reviews. Sleep after stopping is left to cl_can_sleep_stopping and cl_can_stopping_sleep_lab.
